author: froggychairs
cardQuote: LangChain is especially slapped together. Not something I would use in production
quote:
LangChain is especially slapped together. Not something I would use in production (especially with the eval bug that was left unpatched for weeks despite an open PR)

It feels at some point being too slapped together isn’t correlated with success

Wishing the LangChain team well! But there are already alternatives cropping up that are far more polished (Microsoft’s Semantic Kernel being one)
outcome: LangChain became a unicorn, raising $125M at a $1.25B valuation in October 2025.
outcomeDetail: Despite complaints about brittle abstractions and production readiness, LangChain's open-source framework reached roughly 149k GitHub stars, and the company raised a $125M Series B led by IVP at a $1.25B valuation. Its LangSmith observability product became a real revenue line.
note: The critic was right that the codebase was slapped together and risky for production, but wrong that this would sink the company: distribution and the LangSmith business carried it to unicorn status.

author: startupsfail
cardQuote: I think LangChain is already outdated and it (and its copycats) are going to cripple the entire field.
quote: I think LangChain is already outdated and it (and its copycats) are going to cripple the entire field.
outcome: LangChain instead became a standard LLM app framework and a $1.25B company.
outcomeDetail: LangChain's open-source repository reached about 149k GitHub stars, and the company raised $125M at a $1.25B valuation in October 2025. It did not cripple the field; it helped standardize it, even as many teams later moved to lighter patterns.
note: The prediction that LangChain was 'already outdated' and would 'cripple the entire field' was backwards: it became the on-ramp for a generation of LLM apps.

author: popcorncowboy
cardQuote: They raised a 10M seed on what is (no disrespect intended) a wafer thin abstraction that an experienced dev really could implement the core of in a few days.
quote: This is what blows my mind. They raised a 10M seed on what is (no disrespect intended) a wafer thin abstraction that an experienced dev really could implement the core of in a few days. Obviously the raise was about the momentum and mindshare Langchain holds, but still. Wow.
outcome: The 'wafer thin' framework still became a unicorn and a standard entry point for LLM apps.
outcomeDetail: LangChain's core abstractions were indeed simple enough to reimplement, and many teams did. But the project's mindshare, integrations, and LangSmith business helped it reach a $1.25B valuation in 2025.
note: The critic correctly identified the thin technical moat; the miss was assuming a thin moat meant no business. LangChain monetized orchestration and observability rather than the wrapper itself.

author: luckyt
cardQuote: right now LlamaIndex is a mess and makes building things harder instead of easier and it's probably simpler to roll your own solution from scratch.
quote:
Yea, this was my experience too when I tried it out last week for my side project. It's easy to get started, but it's quite complex and disorganized and poorly documented. There are usually several ways to do things (which is by design, since it's meant to give you flexibility of either going with the default or customizing).

The main problem is the documentation is too disorganized, it's hard to figure out what even is the default and what are the configuration options, documentation is spread over a bunch of tutorials, reference pages, and blog posts by the founder. Sometimes the example code doesn't quite work because the library is changing so quickly.

We'll see if the community can figure out the best set of useful abstractions for this domain -- right now LlamaIndex is a mess and makes building things harder instead of easier and it's probably simpler to roll your own solution from scratch. However, the founders seem pretty smart, so hopefully with some time, they'll improve it and make it more usable.
storyTitle: LlamaIndex: Unleash the power of LLMs over your data
outcome: LlamaIndex cleaned up its documentation and raised a $19M Series A in March 2025.
outcomeDetail: LlamaIndex grew to about 53k GitHub stars and became a widely used RAG and data framework; it raised a $19M Series A led by Norwest in 2025, bringing total funding to $27.5M. Documentation and API stability improved, though the framework remains large and fast-moving.
note: The complaint about disorganized docs and rapid breaking changes was accurate, but 'roll your own' underestimated the value of maintained connectors, parsing, and a supported RAG stack.

author: ramoz
cardQuote: I doubt this is a library that can support you beyond prototyping.
quote:
If you’re doing legitimate retrieval rerank in the commercial enterprise setting, then I doubt this is a library that can support you beyond prototyping.

Retrieval involves complex integration (not just data connectors and open API wrappers), and meaningful rerank requires domain/context-specific trained models (that you can deploy performantly and cost effectively). If you’re doing these things, you’re well beyond the capability at platform scale vs what a python library provides
storyTitle: LlamaIndex: Unleash the power of LLMs over your data
outcome: LlamaIndex became a production RAG platform and raised $19M in 2025.
outcomeDetail: The library expanded into LlamaCloud and LlamaParse for enterprise document parsing and retrieval, and the company raised a $19M Series A. Enterprises do use it beyond prototyping, though often alongside custom retrieval code.
note: The critic was right that a Python library alone does not solve enterprise retrieval integration and reranking; LlamaIndex's answer was to build managed parsing and cloud services on top.

author: tw1984
cardQuote: I don't think such business model is going to last. There is no reason for AI giants like OpenAI to stick with such external "vector databases".
quote: I don't think such business model is going to last. There is no reason for AI giants like OpenAI to stick with such external "vector databases". There is not much technical stuff there. Unless you want to argue that "vector searching" is just some labor work when compared to AI, in that case, sure.
storyTitle: Qdrant, the Vector Search Database, raised $28M in a Series A round
outcome: Qdrant kept growing and raised a $50M Series B in March 2026.
outcomeDetail: Qdrant's open-source vector database passed 35k GitHub stars; the company raised a $50M Series B led by AVP in March 2026, bringing total funding to about $88M. Dedicated vector search remained a real market despite consolidation into general databases.
note: The prediction that the business model 'is not going to last' was wrong: Qdrant raised a larger round two years later. The critic was right that vector search is not magic, but wrong that this made it a non-business.

author: lettergram
cardQuote: the whole “vector search database” rush is insane.
quote:
Not to knock Qdrsnt, but generally the whole “vector search database” rush is insane.

I’ve been working with vectors for over a decade; particularly with embeddings used in AI. We’re talking projects from 100k to 100B+ records, used for AI applications

Postgres, particularly with pgvector and derivatives, can handle to millions of records very rapidly no problem. It’s very cheap, scales great, and is accurate.

I’m sure some of these open source solutions are improvements. That said, weigh vendor lock in, cost, risk and in the end it usually makes very little sense.
storyTitle: Qdrant, the Vector Search Database, raised $28M in a Series A round
outcome: Qdrant grew to a $50M Series B, though pgvector remained the default for many teams.
outcomeDetail: Qdrant raised a $50M Series B in 2026 and remained a leading dedicated vector DB. Meanwhile Postgres and pgvector absorbed a large share of simple retrieval workloads, exactly as the critic predicted.
note: The critic was right that pgvector would handle many use cases and that vendor lock-in matters; the miss was writing off the entire dedicated-vector-database category.

author: jillesvangurp
cardQuote: the 28M round suggests a moat that I'm not seeing that clearly in terms of tech. What's so special about qdrant relative to their competition?
quote:
There are a few more. Pinecone comes to mind.

And then there are traditional databases and search products that are integrating vector search capabilities as well: Postgres, Elasticsearch, Opensearch, Solr.

They each have their limitations of course but the 28M round suggests a moat that I'm not seeing that clearly in terms of tech. What's so special about qdrant relative to their competition?

At least they are Apache licensed for now. So, that's nice. But that also means e.g. Apache Lucene could borrow some code from them to beef up their vector search capabilities. Which would benefit Elasticsearch, Opensearch, and Solr which all depend on Lucene.

Which raises the question what the point is of QDrant long term and why investors are betting on this as opposed to other things.

It seems to me that the main challenge with vector search is inference cost (at index and query time), not storing the vectors. A secondary concern is the vector comparisons at query time. A good way to cut down on that is to reduce the overall result set using traditional search or query mechanisms. In other words, you need
storyTitle: Qdrant, the Vector Search Database, raised $28M in a Series A round
outcome: Qdrant's moat was questioned at $28M; it raised $50M two years later.
outcomeDetail: The $28M Series A was followed by a $50M Series B in March 2026. Qdrant differentiated on performance, its Rust implementation, and operational features, but competition from Postgres, Elasticsearch, and Lucene remained intense.
note: The critic correctly saw that vector storage would be absorbed by incumbent databases and that open-source code could be borrowed. Qdrant's counter was execution and focus, not a unique algorithm.

author: 0xbadc0de5
cardQuote: But to do anything useful, you're going to want a powerful GPU (RTX 3090, RTX 4090 or A6000) with as much VRAM as possible.
quote:
That's all fine and good. But to do anything useful, you're going to want a powerful GPU (RTX 3090, RTX 4090 or A6000) with as much VRAM as possible. Unlike the diffusion models, LLM's are very memory-intensive, even at 4-bit GPTQ. The larger models like llama-13b and llama-30b run quite well at 4-bit on a 24GB GPU. The llama-65b-4bit should run on a dual 3090/4090 rig.

Coupled with the leaked Bing prompt and text-generation-webui, the results are quite impressive.
storyTitle: Llama.cpp: Port of Facebook's LLaMA model in C/C++, with Apple Silicon support
outcome: llama.cpp became the standard local LLM runtime, with 134k+ GitHub stars.
outcomeDetail: llama.cpp's GGUF format and CPU/Apple Silicon inference became the foundation for Ollama, LM Studio, and many other local AI tools. The project has 134k+ GitHub stars and is still actively developed.
note: The comment said a powerful GPU was required 'to do anything useful'; llama.cpp proved that quantized CPU and unified-memory inference was useful enough to create the entire local-LLM category.

author: amelius
cardQuote: Why did they focus on a specific model rather than a generic solution that makes ANY python based model work on Apple silicon?
quote: Yes this is a good question. Why did they focus on a specific model rather than a generic solution that makes ANY python based model work on Apple silicon?
storyTitle: Llama.cpp: Port of Facebook's LLaMA model in C/C++, with Apple Silicon support
outcome: llama.cpp became a generic runtime for countless model families, not just LLaMA.
outcomeDetail: The project expanded from LLaMA to a general GGUF-based inference engine supporting Qwen, Mistral, Gemma, DeepSeek, and multimodal models. Its 134k+ stars make it one of the most-used local inference projects.
note: The critic asked why the author did not build a generic Python-model solution; llama.cpp's answer was a generic C/C++ runtime and file format that outlived the original model.

author: elwebmaster
cardQuote: Mixtral > Codellama > DeepSeek Coder. Very weird model, writes super long comments on one line, definitely not at the level of Codellama, benchmarks be damned.
quote: Mixtral > Codellama > DeepSeek Coder. Very weird model, writes super long comments on one line, definitely not at the level of Codellama, benchmarks be damned.
storyTitle: DeepSeek Coder: Let the Code Write Itself
outcome: DeepSeek's models became frontier contenders; DeepSeek-R1 wiped about $600B off Nvidia in January 2025.
outcomeDetail: DeepSeek Coder V2 beat GPT-4 Turbo on coding benchmarks by June 2024, and DeepSeek-R1 became the top free app in the US App Store in January 2025, triggering a record one-day market-cap loss at Nvidia. DeepSeek was valued at $52B in May 2026.
note: The comment ranked DeepSeek Coder below Mixtral and CodeLlama and dismissed its benchmarks; within five months DeepSeek Coder V2 was beating GPT-4 Turbo, and within a year DeepSeek had reshaped the AI market.

author: Giorgi
cardQuote: In what world "comparable", looks like another Chinese ChatGPT "alternative" that is a crap.
quote: In what world "comparable", looks like another Chinese ChatGPT "alternative" that is a crap.
storyTitle: DeepSeek v2.5 – open-source LLM comparable to GPT-4, but 95% less expensive
outcome: Three months later DeepSeek-R1 became a global sensation and DeepSeek reached a $52B valuation.
outcomeDetail: DeepSeek-R1 launched in January 2025, topped the US App Store, and helped erase about $593B from Nvidia's market value in a day. DeepSeek raised a $7B round at a $52B post-money valuation in May 2026.
note: Calling DeepSeek 'another Chinese ChatGPT alternative that is a crap' was a spectacular miss: it became the model that forced the frontier labs to cut prices and rethink training costs.

author: Eridrus
cardQuote: I have a lot of skepticism that this is a long term business.
quote:
People keep saying that training is tricky, which is true, you need people with experience, but they're not so rare that this will present a moat forever since you can very much hire the people who know how to do this.

My experience with ML projects is that while there is churn in the modeling, most of the effort for a long lived system still goes into the data, but engineers really want to work on the modeling/infra pieces much more than data quality.

Which is to say, I have a lot of skepticism that this is a long term business.
storyTitle: Together AI raises a $102.5M Series A
outcome: Together AI became an AI neocloud worth $8.3B after an $800M Series C in July 2026.
outcomeDetail: Together AI raised $305M at a $3.3B valuation in February 2025, then $800M at $8.3B in July 2026. Its training and inference business scaled with the open-model boom, even as price competition remained brutal.
note: The critic was right that training know-how is hireable and that inference is competitive; the miss was underestimating how much demand and capital would flow to independent GPU clouds.

author: datadrivenangel
cardQuote: when TogetherAI flops and returns five cents on the investment dollar write it off in a different line of business?
quote:
I wonder how NVIDIA gets to report their investment here from an accounting perspective?

Could they book the money TogetherAI spends on GPUs as revenue now, and then when TogetherAI flops and returns five cents on the investment dollar write it off in a different line of business?
storyTitle: Together AI raises a $102.5M Series A
outcome: Together AI did not flop; it reached an $8.3B valuation in 2026.
outcomeDetail: Together AI's revenue and valuation grew through the open-model and inference boom, culminating in an $800M Series C at $8.3B in July 2026. Nvidia's investment was part of a broader strategic relationship, not a write-off.
note: The comment predicted TogetherAI would 'flop and return five cents on the investment dollar'; instead it became one of the largest independent AI clouds.

author: brucethemoose2
cardQuote: Civitai's enshittification potential is sky high. They are hosting loads of enormous models and images for free, on a very spiffy, heavy website. There's no way thats sustainable.
quote:
I disagree with the tone of the headline. CivitAI is a good resource, and the rest of AI world could learn from it for, for example, LLM lora/grammar hosting.

But I am concerned, for a different reason.

Civitai's enshittification potential is sky high. They are hosting loads of enormous models and images for free, on a very spiffy, heavy website. There's no way thats sustainable.
storyTitle: Andreessen Horowitz Invests in Civitai, Which Profits from Nonconsensual AI Porn
outcome: Civitai grew to 23M+ monthly accesses and remained a leading AI model-sharing site, but faced hosting and payment risk.
outcomeDetail: Civitai reached 3M registered users by November 2023 and 23.2M monthly accesses by April 2024, backed by Andreessen Horowitz. It later faced provider and payment-processor pressure over moderation, validating the sustainability concern even as the platform survived.
note: The critic was right that free hosting of enormous models and images was financially fragile, and Civitai later ran into provider and payment trouble. But the site's network effect kept it at the center of the Stable Diffusion ecosystem.

author: behnamoh
cardQuote: Please don't release new models unless there is an arch change. All these new LLMs are essentially the same technique applied to almost the same dataset.
quote: Please don't release new models unless there is an arch change. All these new LLMs are essentially the same technique applied to almost the same dataset.
outcome: Qwen became the world's most-downloaded open model family, with 1B+ downloads.
outcomeDetail: Alibaba's Qwen family passed 700M Hugging Face downloads by January 2026 and over 1B downloads later that year, with more than 200,000 derivative models. Qwen3 and Qwen3.8 became leading open-weight releases.
note: The comment dismissed Qwen2 as 'essentially the same technique' and not worth releasing; Qwen's rapid iteration made it the most widely fine-tuned open model family in the world.
